title: 50th sitting of the 20th Majlis (Continuation)
presiding: Speaker Abdul Raheem Abdulla (Fonadhoo); Deputy Speaker Ahmed Nazim chaired after the 10:29-11:07 break until the Speaker resumed the chair
summary: This part continues the debate on the proposed 2025 state budget of about 56.6 billion rufiyaa, with twelve members taking the floor in the first hours of the sitting. Most speakers backed the budget, pointing to its record housing allocation, health and education spending and a smaller deficit, and listed projects for their islands. Members for Maavashu and Meedhoo criticised the lack of island-by-island detail, and several members complained of unfinished projects left by earlier governments. The sitting paused from 10:29 to 11:07; no vote is recorded in this part, and the text ends partway through the Kendhikulhudhoo member's speech. This part is the continuing general debate on the government's proposed 2025 state budget, with the Finance Minister listening in the house. A member's speech that began in part 1 ends, then members for North Hulhumale', Vaikaradhoo, Kanditheemu, South Hulhumale', Maradhoo, Thoddoo and Funadhoo speak. Opposition-side members criticised missing project-level detail, the planned subsidy cuts and growing debt, while government-side members defended the budget as honouring presidential pledges, and the two sides traded claims over past debt. No vote was held; the house took a prayer recess and a longer afternoon recess because about 12 more members still wanted to speak. The text is partly garbled, so some details are approximate. This part continues the general debate on the government's 2025 state budget (about MVR 56.6 billion). Government-aligned members backed the budget and pointed to fiscal reform, the president's promises and past debts, while MDP members criticised heavy taxes and borrowing, cuts to Aasandha and council block grants, and the lack of project-level detail. The debate closed after 77 members had spoken for 14 hours 17 minutes. The budget now goes to the Budget Committee before a vote, and the sitting was adjourned to 20 November 2024 at 9:00. The part opens mid-speech with a member whose header is in an earlier part, so that speaker is not listed.

items.title: Debate on the 2025 state budget (general debate, continued)
items.outcome: debated; debate closed after 77 members spoke; goes to the Budget Committee, then a floor vote

speakers.name: Ahmed Shakir
positions: Said Laamu Atoll islands have been neglected by every government and that the budget book does not show island-level projects.
Described islands without sewerage and patient transport that takes days, citing constitutional equality and basic-rights articles.
Said he would take a leap of faith with the budget while urging the government to act on these gaps.

speakers.name: Ahmed Siyam Mohamed
positions: Said the budget book lacks details for islands and projects, so members cannot debate it properly, and asked for it to be reissued.
Criticised a 40% rise in spending on foreign embassies and subsidies to state companies, urging cuts.
Said members were not consulted and that he would not vote for the budget as submitted.

speakers.name: Ahmed Naseer
positions: Supported the budget, citing health and education allocations and cuts to state spending.
Said Ihavandhoo lacks sewerage and a children's doctor, and land reclamation there is unfinished.
Expected the planned hospital and a fish collection centre to proceed under this budget.

speakers.name: Mohamed Dawoodh
positions: Gave budget figures: 49.2 billion spending, 9.4 billion deficit, and said it is the smallest deficit share of GDP since 2019.
Listed repeatedly budgeted but unfinished Kulhudhuffushi projects (hospital, housing, harbour, water plant, airport, sports) and asked that contractors be held accountable.
Welcomed the housing loan scheme, noting many residents own idle plots and need finance to build.

speakers.name: Ali Moosa
positions: Said the deficit is lower than in earlier years but questioned financing it through loans and interest payments, and linked the budget to national sovereignty.
Said council allocations for Hoarafushi, Uligamu and Thuraakunu rose and local projects are being paid for and progressing.
Cited about 123 billion rufiyaa in national debt and unpaid state-company bills left by previous governments.

speakers.name: Hussain Shareef
positions: Said housing is the central issue for the budget and described long-waiting Hulhumale' North residents left out of earlier flat allocations.
Argued the current government's housing towers are nearly complete and that the budget is built to secure housing for citizens.
Defended the budget and urged members to judge past governments' delivery on health, education and housing promises.

speakers.name: Dr. Ahmed Shamheed
positions: Thanked the government for extra funding for Hulhumale' health services and said the area needs a large hospital.
Said budget details are hidden, citing the Constitution and the Public Finance Act, and noted recurrent spending exceeded revenue.
Replied to government claims about debt by citing external debt figures under earlier administrations and defended the 2020 currency decisions.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Nazil
positions: Said the budget lacks project-level detail and that recurrent spending takes 63% of it.
Raised concern over Aasandha and subsidy cuts and reduced council block grants.
Said promised Addu City works, such as the Hithadhoo harbour and a fish factory, have stalled.

speakers.name: Mohamed Shamin Habeeb
positions: Described flooding in Kurendhoo and long-stalled harbour, sewerage and building works there and in nearby islands.
Supported the 5% housing loans and said the government should get one to two years before results are judged.
Called for people who took public money improperly to be taken to court and the money recovered.

speakers.name: Ismail Shafeeu
positions: Backed the budget as a hopeful one that would solve housing and let stalled projects restart.
Expected Isdhoo-Kalaidhoo road paving, airport work and conversion of the health centre into a hospital to start.

speakers.name: Faruhath Mohamed
positions: Supported the budget, citing housing units, the regional hospital, roads and electricity works for Kulhudhuffushi.
Raised school overcrowding and stalled school buildings in Kulhudhuffushi, and the stadium track upgrade.

speakers.name: Mohamed Ismail
positions: Called it a complete budget and listed revenue measures such as airport tax, green tax and higher cigarette duty.
Compared budgets and debt across earlier governments with the present one, saying this government inherited heavy debt.
Cited Vilimale' projects including a tertiary hospital, roads and a petrol shed, and housing as the main priority.

speakers.name: Hussain Nasih
positions: Backed the budget as the most complete so far, designed to benefit the whole country.
Highlighted housing spending, the Rasmale eco-city, and health and education allocations.
Said stopping money printing and projected growth of about 6.4% show a firmer economic course.

speakers.name: Ali Ibrahim
positions: Said it is the first budget presented under the public finance law and is focused on housing, including 1,500 housing units in 2025 and loans in the Malé area.

speakers.name: Mohamed Afoo Hamid
positions: Called the budget practical and realistic, noting inherited debt of over 120 billion rufiyaa.
Highlighted a record housing allocation, Islamic-principle housing loans and reform of state companies.
Raised Kendhikulhudhoo-area needs: sewerage, coastal protection at Maalhendhoo and a health centre at Kudafari.

speakers.name: Hussain Ziyad
positions: Said the budget is about MVR 1bn larger than this year's but lacks project-level detail, citing the house rules on detailed information.
Questioned how direct subsidies would be targeted and what subsidy cuts would mean for electricity and ticket prices.
Asked what Vaikaradhoo and nearby islands will get from the PSIP allocation, saying he saw no firm project details.

speakers.name: Ameen Faisal
positions: Said the budget gives members different hopes but no island-level project breakdown for Kanditheemu or Shaviyani atoll.
Pointed to stalled works such as harbours, a multipurpose hall and classrooms and asked when promised projects would be delivered.
Welcomed some allocations for health centres, roads and harbours but wanted clear figures for each island.

speakers.name: Ahmed Didi
positions: Called the budget directionless and tax and debt heavy, saying it gives no detail on how money will be spent.
Said cutting fuel and electricity subsidies would raise prices and hurt fishers, businesses and households.
Listed Maradhoo needs (link road, health centre, school hall, Addu projects) and said he could not support the budget.

speakers.name: Hussain Sameer
positions: Criticised the budget as burdening residents and said it will add heavily to national debt.
Said government-side members had not spoken up for their constituents on subsidy cuts and cost of living.
Raised Thoddoo concerns such as a single doctor at the health centre and the size of council block grants.

speakers.name: Mohamed Mamdooh
positions: Said this is the first budget presented in line with the Constitution and financial laws and that its details are in the budget book.
Argued earlier budgets under the previous Majlis had small, scattered project allocations and low release rates.
Defended the Aasandha and ENSPA changes and said the budget is designed to deliver the president's pledges.

speakers.name: Abdul Latheef Mohamed
positions: Said he fully backs the 2025 budget and compared it with how earlier MDP-era budgets and debts were handled.

speakers.name: Ahmed Azaan Marzooq
positions: Backed the budget's fiscal reform aims: pension, Aasandha and subsidy reform, and tighter management of state companies.
Defended the program-style budget, saying it sets goals and priorities instead of listing every project.
Said the government is prioritising Addu City's livelihood problems, including through housing loans.

speakers.name: Mohamed Niushad
positions: Called the budget heavy on taxes, spending and debt, and said it hides where project money goes.
Criticised cuts to council block grants and Aasandha and the growth in political appointees and fixed-asset spending.
Said promised works in his constituency, such as land reclamation and a school building, were not delivered in 2024.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Shujau
positions: Backed the budget as the first aligned with IMF principles and defended the government's debt and spending record.
Said PSIP projects are the president's promises and that spending was cut and revenue raised without printing money.
Listed priorities for his islands, such as a ring road, health centre upgrade and fishing jetty, saying locals should choose.

speakers.name: Ali Ashrag
positions: Called the budget thorough and said it was drawn up after the president visited islands to hear needs.
Said it funds works in his constituency, including Kinbidhoo land reclamation and Hirilandhoo cold storage and revetment.
Urged members to pass the budget as the president requested.

speakers.name: Ali Fazad
positions: Welcomed the targets of direct debt at 95% of GDP and a primary deficit under 5% of GDP by 2026.
Listed Fuvahmulah projects budgeted in 2020 to 2023 that he said were never built.
Backed targeted subsidies and hoped the government can protect the MVR 7 billion in budgeted savings.

speakers.name: Ahmed Thariq
positions: Said the budget does not conflict with the Constitution or law and answered criticism about missing detail.
Warned that 2025 and 2026 are tight years for debt payments and urged restructuring debts with the two largest creditors.
Urged talks with businesspeople on the dollar shortage and new tourism markets as taxes rise.

decisions: Chair announced the budget debate would continue until all registered members had spoken, with sign-up open until 9:30.
Chair gave each member 15 minutes and recessed for midday prayer (11:57 to 13:01).
Chair recessed the sitting from 14:03 and resumed at 17:01 because about 12 more members still wished to speak.
Budget debate continued with no motion put to a vote in this part.
General debate on the 2025 state budget closed after 77 members spoke over 14 hours 17 minutes.
The Budget Committee will now decide on the budget and return it to the floor for a vote.
Sitting adjourned until Wednesday 20 November 2024 at 9:00.
